- **0** means they are unrelated.

So 0.10 says passage B is almost unrelated to the question. In the lesson's example, "expense claim" scored 0.12 against "parental leave". That is about how far off B is. Sending B to the LLM (the language model that writes the answer) would give it text that has little to do with the question. Search ranks passages by cosine from highest to lowest, so B would land near the bottom.

**Why A is better:** at 0.95, passage A points almost the same way as the question, so it most likely means nearly the same thing and can help answer it.

check:0:2.a:
"Neither: cosine measures length" has the idea backwards. Cosine similarity deliberately ignores length. It only asks which way two vectors point.

There is one small grain of truth in it. Length does show up in the calculation. You multiply the numbers position by position, add them up, then divide by the two vectors' lengths. But that division is there to *cancel* length out, not to measure it. What's left is purely about direction.

Picture two arrows on a map. One is short, one is long. If they point the same way, cosine says they match. That's why a short question can still match a long passage.

So the option misses the main point. A score of 0.95 is not a statement about size. It says the question and passage A point almost the same way. In embedding terms, that means they mean nearly the same thing. A score of 0.10 says passage B points somewhere nearly unrelated.

Passage A is the better answer because its cosine of 0.95 means its meaning lies very close to the question's, so it most likely holds what the question is asking about.

check:1:1.q: Why not “The newer model is broken”?
check:1:1.a:
It's a fair first guess. The results did get worse right after the switch, so blaming the new model feels natural. But that guess misses what actually went wrong.

The newer model is probably fine. If you embedded both your documents and your questions with it, search would likely work well, maybe even better than before.

The real problem is mixing. Each model learns its own space on its own. Nobody chose what each dimension means, so position 5 in the old model's vector has nothing to do with position 5 in the new one. The two models might not even give the same count of numbers.

So cosine similarity, which compares direction, is now comparing arrows drawn on two different maps. The scores come out as numbers, but they mean nothing. The "nearest" passage is just noise.

The fix shows it isn't a broken model. Re-embed all your documents with the new model, or keep using the old model for questions. Either way, everything lives in one space again.

"The two models' spaces don't match" is better because it names the real cause: vectors are only comparable when the same model made them.

judge.notes: No real problems. Small nit: it says the scores 'come out as numbers' while also suggesting the vectors might have different lengths, in which case cosine couldn't be computed at all.

check:1:2.q: Why not “The documents got too long”?
check:1:2.a:
"The documents got too long" sounds reasonable, but it doesn't fit what happened.

First, the documents didn't change. The only thing that changed was the model used for the questions. If results were fine before the switch and nonsense after, the cause has to be the switch.

Second, length isn't what breaks search here. An embedding model gives the same count of numbers for any text, short or long. And cosine similarity compares direction, not length, so a long passage can still match a short question.

It does get one small thing right. Very long text can blur its meaning, and models have an input limit, so text past that point gets cut off. But that would make results slightly worse, not turn them into nonsense overnight.

The real issue is that each model learns its own space. Its dimensions (the positions in the list of numbers) mean different things. Comparing a vector from one model with a vector from another is like reading coordinates from two different maps.

"The two models' spaces don't match" is better because it points at the one thing that changed, and that change makes every comparison meaningless.

judge.notes: The input-limit and 'blur its meaning' claims are not in the lesson, though they do not contradict it. Otherwise the answer is accurate and under 200 words.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Yes: long passages always score low”?
check:2:1.a:
**"Yes: long passages always score low" doesn't fit how cosine similarity works.**

It does catch one real thing. A long passage often covers several ideas. Its embedding (the list of numbers standing for its meaning) then blends those ideas, so it may match a narrow question less sharply. But that comes from mixed meaning, not from length. And it doesn't happen "always".

Here is what it misses. The text's length doesn't change how many numbers you get. A two-line question and a two-page passage both become 1,536 numbers. Cosine similarity then divides by each vector's length, where "length" means how big the arrow is, not how many words the text had. Dividing like that removes size from the score, so only the direction is left. A long text gains no advantage and takes no penalty just for being long.

The question also tells you the score is 0.9. That's close to 1, so the two point almost the same way. That is a strong match, not a low score.

**"No: cosine compares direction, not length"** is better because it names the actual rule: the score depends on which way the arrows point, so a short question and a long passage can match well.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Yes: the question must be longer”?
check:2:2.a:
That option starts from a fair instinct. A two-line question and a two-page passage look very different, so it seems natural to worry that the short one can't "match" the long one. It's also true that a very short text gives the model less to go on.

But it misses how cosine similarity works. Every text, short or long, becomes a vector of the same size: 1,536 numbers. Cosine similarity only asks whether two vectors point the same way. It ignores how long they are. So the question doesn't need to be longer to be compared fairly.

The score already answers the question. A cosine of 0.9 is close to 1, which means the two vectors point in nearly the same direction. In plain words, the question and the passage are about the same thing. Padding the question with extra words wouldn't fix anything, because nothing is broken. It could even blur the meaning and lower the match.

"No: cosine compares direction, not length" is better because it names the actual rule: cosine scores whether two arrows point the same way, so a short question and a long passage can match strongly.

judge.notes: The claims that a short text gives the model less to go on and that padding could lower the match come from outside the lesson. They are plausible and hedged, and they don't contradict it.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Dot product over the lengths, then keep the best” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second answer**

*The problem:* "A user asks a question. I need the passage that means the same thing, even if it uses different words."

*The idea:* "Every text becomes an embedding, a list of numbers. I compare the question to each passage with cosine similarity. That's the dot product, meaning multiply matching positions and add them up. Then I divide by the two vectors' lengths, which is each vector's overall size. Dividing removes size, so only direction counts. I walk through the passages once and keep the highest score."

*Edge case:* "If a vector is all zeros, its length is zero and the division breaks, so I'd guard against that. Also, an internal product code the model never learned may score low even when it's the right match."

**A likely follow-up**

"Why divide at all? Why not just use the dot product?"

*Hint:* Without dividing, a vector with bigger numbers can score higher just for being bigger, not for meaning the same thing. Dividing keeps the comparison fair between a short question and a long passage. A strong answer says direction carries the meaning, not size, like two arrows on a map.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **A score above 1.** Cosine tops out at 1, meaning "same direction". A bigger number means the step of dividing by the two vectors' lengths was skipped.
- **The longest passage keeps winning.** Without that division, long passages get big totals just for having bigger numbers, not for matching meaning. A short, exact answer loses to a long, rambling one.
- **Questions with internal terms come back with unrelated passages.** A product code the model never learned may land nowhere useful. Its nearest passage is just the least-bad guess, often with a low score.
- **The LLM answers confidently from the wrong passage.** The LLM answers from what retrieval returns. If the top passage is off, the answer is off.

**Quickest check**

Score a few pairs where you already know the answer, like the lesson's example. "Parental leave" vs "maternity leave" should score high, and vs "expense claim" should score near 0. Also score one text against itself: it should be exactly 1. Then try a short and a long passage that say the same thing. Both should score about the same against the question.

learn:stops.a:
**1. Words the model never learned.** Internal product codes, ticket numbers or team slang may land nowhere useful, so the right passage scores low. Add keyword search alongside it (often called **hybrid search**, meaning you combine exact-word matching with meaning matching).

**2. Switching embedding models.** Each model builds its own space, so a vector from one model means nothing next to a vector from another. If you upgrade the model, re-embed every passage, and always embed questions with the same model as the passages.

**3. A very large number of passages.** Comparing the question with every passage one by one is fine for hundreds, but gets slow for millions. Use a **vector index**, a structure that finds near neighbours without checking them all, such as Databricks Vector Search.

A related caution: "closest" is not always "correct." Text like "leave is allowed" and "leave is not allowed" can score very close. So return a few top passages, not just one, and let the LLM read them.

learn:term.a:
A **vector** is just the container. It's an ordered list of numbers, like `[0.12, -0.40, 0.88, ...]`. On its own it says nothing about meaning. A vector could hold anything: temperatures, prices, pixel colours.

An **embedding** is a vector made by a model from text, so that its position captures meaning. Every embedding is a vector, but not every vector is an embedding. "Embed" is also the verb: you embed a question to get its vector.

**An everyday comparison:** a vector is like a pair of map coordinates. Any two numbers make coordinates. An embedding is the coordinates of a real café, chosen so that similar cafés sit nearby.

**How they work together:** `text-embedding-3-small` embeds "parental leave" into a vector of 1,536 numbers. It does the same for "maternity leave." Because both are vectors, you can compare them with cosine similarity. That measures whether two arrows point the same way, ignoring their length. Here it gives 0.91, nearly the same direction. "Expense claim" scores 0.12, far off.

The model supplies the meaning. The vector gives you something you can do maths on.

judge.notes: Minor: the café analogy is a little loose (café locations aren't chosen to cluster), and the 0.91 and 0.12 scores are the lesson's example numbers but are stated as if the model really output them.
